pages.1: A proposal to the NHS Patient Entrepreneur Programme, Cohort 4. Connecting the Dots. Paving the way towards our National Care Service. Our pilot tests whether connected support helps carers and the people they care for return to work sooner, improves outcomes and generates cost evidence to help fund a future connected National Care Service. The Care Collective.
pages.2: The problem we are solving. By connecting the dots. Carers are left to connect the dots. Government agencies often work in separate systems. Information and responsibility do not reliably travel with the person, so families are left to repeat their story, chase updates and coordinate handovers themselves. Forty-nine percent of delayed discharges after stays of fourteen days or longer were linked to social care capacity, transfer delays or access to rehabilitation and recovery. Twenty-six point eight percent of surveyed unpaid carers found it fairly or very difficult to find information or advice about support, services or benefits. Twenty point nine percent said they had no encouragement or support in their caring role. Sources: CQC and NHS England, March 2025, and the DHSC Survey of Adult Carers in England, 2025 to 2026. What the pilot tests: connect the handovers, not just the services. In five locations, the pilot will test whether named handovers and a shared picture of each family's needs reduce the coordination burden. The time carers currently spend navigating the system can instead go to their own lives, wellbeing, learning, training or work, and to the person they care for.
pages.3: Connecting the Dots. How to Fund Our National Care Service. Two national services. One connected life. A co-produced proposition to connect health, care and opportunity around people, and test the economic value of better outcomes. Prepared by Aubrey Ghose, unpaid carer and Richmond and Wandsworth co-production contributor. Pilot first. Platform second. Evidence before scale.
pages.4: The destination. Two national services. One connected life. National Health Service: your health, connected. National Care Service: your care, connected. The Government has committed to establishing a National Care Service. The Casey Commission has been asked to help determine how it should be implemented. The opportunity is to build care as a connected national service, able to work alongside a connected health service. Connect care. Release capacity. Reduce cost. Improve outcomes. Connecting the Dots: a co-produced proposition for the Independent Commission into Adult Social Care.
pages.5: The vision. A National Care Service alongside the NHS. Two national services, working together around the same household. National Health Service: your health, connected. High-quality healthcare, free at the point of use, for everyone in England. National Care Service: your care, connected. One recognisable front door connecting the public services that surround care, around the person who needs it and the people who care for them. What care needs to connect: adult social care, including support, assessment and care services. Housing: safe, suitable and stable homes. DWP and benefits: income, entitlements and financial support. Recovery and rehabilitation: treatment, therapy and long-term support. Mental health: integrated physical and mental health support. Learning and training: skills, confidence and personal development. Community support: voluntary, community and peer support. Employment: support into, in and back to work. One household. Two people. One plan. A more connected life. Connect services and decisions around the household, with consent and clear responsibility.
pages.6: The operating model. One household. One shared three-hundred-and-sixty-degree view. A shared, permissioned view of each care relationship: the household where relevant, never a merged identity. The consenting care relationship includes the carer and the supported person. Each has their own needs, choices and rights. NHS and GPs provide health and treatment. Adult social care provides support and assessments. Mental health provides continuity and recovery. Housing provides stability and safety. DWP and work connect benefits and employment. Voluntary and community organisations and training connect community and opportunity. A shared picture includes relevant information, shared care goals, named owners and next actions. One connected plan and visible accountability. Organise the public services we already have around one goal. See both voices and relevant facts. Act with one lead and explicit next steps. Measure independence, time, work and cost. The National Care Service starts with a shared way of working. The switch is operational, not a claim that IT can be connected overnight: consent, lawful access, shared goals, named owners and measured outcomes. Each agency keeps its legal duties and existing systems.
pages.7: The evidence. What the evidence is built on. Carers, carees, people with lived experience and professionals contributed across a documented process. Eleven meeting dates. Nine official records. Three hundred and thirty-eight source-linked entries. Forty-one named participants. Sixteen directly attributed. Six recurring findings. What people described: repeating information, chasing handovers and coordinating support across services while trying to care. A documented pattern, gathered over three years of co-production. The recurring burden is not a lack of effort by carers. It is the work of joining up support that arrives in separate pieces.
pages.8: The findings. Six recurring findings. Practical changes identified across the Richmond and Wandsworth co-production record. Joined-up services and shared responsibility: make hand-offs and ownership visible across organisational boundaries. One route to accurate information and records: create a reliable route to the right service so carers do not reconstruct the story. Earlier carer support: identify carers early, plan assessment, respite and contingency. Prevention and continuity before crisis: keep support connected through discharge, accommodation and changes in responsibility. Accessible communication: connect people to information while keeping a clear human route and alternatives. Co-production that closes the loop: show what changed because people contributed, with action, owner, date and outcome. Provenance and approval: source, Richmond Borough and Wandsworth co-production records. Findings are offered for working-group confirmation, not as unanimous endorsement. Provenance to be checked before approval.
pages.9: National corroboration. The same six issues appear in national evidence. Joined-up services and shared responsibility: forty-nine percent of delayed discharges after acute stays of fourteen days or longer were linked to social care capacity or transfer delays, twenty-three percent, or access to rehabilitation, reablement or recovery, twenty-six percent. Source: CQC, The State of Health Care and Adult Social Care in England 2024 to 2025, and NHS England data, March 2025. One route to accurate information and records: twenty-six point eight percent of surveyed unpaid carers said it was fairly or very difficult to find information or advice about support, services or benefits. Earlier carer support: twenty point nine percent of surveyed unpaid carers said they had no encouragement or support in their caring role. Source: DHSC, Survey of Adult Carers in England 2025 to 2026. Scope: this survey measures carers' experience of support information. It does not measure shared records or repeated storytelling.
pages.10: National corroboration. The same six issues appear in national evidence. Prevention and continuity before crisis: three hundred and thirty-five thousand new-client requests for adult social care support in 2024 to 2025 originated at hospital discharge, seventeen percent of all such requests. Source: DHSC adult social care activity report. Accessible communication: twelve point one percent of adult social care service users who tried to find information or advice found it very difficult, forty-six thousand seven hundred and sixty people in the survey. Source: DHSC Adult Social Care Survey, 2024 to 2025. Co-production that closes the loop: thirty-eight point one percent of carers who knew discussions about the cared-for person's services had happened said they were always involved or consulted. Source: DHSC Survey of Adult Carers in England, 2025 to 2026. Scope: these indicators corroborate the themes. They do not reproduce the local meeting sample or measure whether feedback changed services.
pages.11: The national system case. Health and care: one system. The NHS feels the cost of a broken handover. Reasons for delayed discharges after fourteen days or longer, England, March 2025. Nearly half, forty-nine percent, were linked to social care capacity, transfers, rehabilitation or recovery. Twenty-three percent: lack of social care capacity or delays completing transfers to social care. Twenty-six percent: delays accessing rehabilitation, reablement or recovery services. Casey's remit recognises the health-care interface. Its terms of reference call for a data-driven review of NHS and council funding at the health-care interface, with reforms to reduce unnecessary hospital admissions and delayed discharges. Connecting the Dots offers a small local test of shared oversight and named handovers: the same system question, measured in practice in Richmond and Wandsworth. Sources: CQC reporting NHS England discharge reasons, March 2025, and Casey Commission terms of reference.
pages.12: The national opportunity. Millions of people. One household at a time. The scale is national, but improvement starts with a practical relationship and a measurable result. Five point eight million unpaid carers in the UK: most recent comparable UK census total, 2021. Many already work or are retired. One point one million left paid work to care: estimated number who left jobs to care in the two years before September 2026, polling, not a census. Eight hundred and eighty-nine thousand people receiving council-arranged long-term support in England during 2024 to 2025. Published figures are subject to planned corrections. Sixteen point seven million disabled people in the UK: a 2024 to 2025 estimate. This is context, not a count of people needing care or suitable for paid work. Twenty-nine point four billion pounds: gross local authority adult social care expenditure in England, 2024 to 2025. This is existing spending, not a sum the pilot can simply redirect. These populations overlap. They must not be added together or treated as a ready-to-work workforce. Sources: Carers UK, DWP Family Resources Survey and DHSC.
pages.13: The architecture. Before we connect the dots, count them. The NHS has stronger internal pathways for its own services. The wider support system crosses organisations with different owners, duties and budgets. Integrated Care System: a local partnership. NHS organisations, councils and other community partners plan together. NHS service architecture is more connected internally, with seams between providers. An Integrated Care Board handles local NHS planning and commissioning. Primary care includes GP practices and primary care networks. Hospitals and specialist services include trusts. Community health includes community teams and services. Mental health includes NHS mental health services. Wider support has distinct owners and routes: council adult social care, council and housing providers, DWP benefits and employment support. One household. Two people: carer and caree. Shared home, shared care: both belong in the support picture. Two people. Two sets of rights. A shared care relationship must never erase either person's needs or identity. Relevant decisions, support and accountability should be visible, with consent and each person's rights respected. Connection is also a human experience. The test will ask carers and people receiving support whether involvement is respectful, accessible and useful, and whether it leads to better decisions.
pages.14: The system benchmark. Two services. One disconnected experience. The NHS is the national reference. Care and wider support are fragmented across organisations. The proposed method connects decisions, not databases. The chart contrasts fragmented care encounters with a proposed connected pathway at the point of connection. The green dots illustrate disconnected care encounters, not a measured time series. Their transition into one pathway is the proposed bridge towards care working alongside the NHS. The six local findings and national evidence describe the barriers this pilot would address. Conceptual model, not measured results or a forecast.
pages.15: The pilot: scale and place. A one-hundred-family pilot across five locations. Twenty families in each location, including Richmond and Wandsworth as one borough. One hundred families in total. Five pilot locations. Twenty families per location. Newcastle, Manchester, Birmingham, Bristol, and Richmond and Wandsworth. How it will work: connect relevant services, name the handovers, measure before and after. What the spread adds: testing in five places creates the opportunity to learn across a wider mix of communities, demographics and local service settings. Equal groups make it easier to compare delivery, see what works consistently and identify where local adaptation is needed. This is a feasibility and early-outcomes pilot, not a nationally representative sample.
pages.16: A learning system for the pilot. Learn across services, in real time. A light-touch, AI-enabled workflow could help each local team connect agreed information, notice patterns and improve handovers across its twenty participating families. Capture: families and staff agree a shared goal plan and what information can be used. Connect: a simple local workflow supports named handovers and flags gaps for staff to review. Learn: an AI-supported view groups feedback and outcomes to reveal recurring barriers and patterns. Patterns, progress and staff feedback, together. Show progress towards family goals, recurring handover gaps, service feedback and emerging outcomes across locations. Staff review the signals. The system supports coordination and learning, not care decisions. At six months, review efficacy, delivery cost, family and staff experience, and whether to continue or expand the test.
pages.17: The proposition. Carers Connect. One connected front door to health, care, home and work. The concept image shows a person holding the NCS app, with connections to home, people, health, records, education and work. One household. Two people. One plan. A more connected life. A practical service concept: the right information, the right handover and the right support, in one everyday place. Concept visual: a proposed service, not a current government application.
pages.18: Prove the method. Start with achievable gains. Then tackle harder barriers. All households receive support from the outset. The stages describe what outcomes we can test and learn from first. Early gains: keep or restore paid hours. Help willing carers resolve missed information, repeated assessments, coordination delays and barriers to flexible work. Measure hours of paid work retained or regained and time saved. Next opportunities: learning, training and supported work. Coordinate rehabilitation, transport, benefits advice, employment support and accessible training where the person wants them. Measure new participation, confidence, skills and work readiness. Complex needs: stability before employability. For families facing multiple risks or high care needs, join decisions across health, housing and support. Do not make employment a condition of care. Measure continuity, avoided crises, independence and wellbeing. This page states twenty consenting households, ten plus ten, six months. Baseline first. Track change in every household. Record harms and non-improvements. Independent review.
pages.19: The outcomes hypothesis. Connect care. Improve lives. The third pathway makes the test visible: when health and care decisions connect, can recovery, independence, learning and work improve? The diagram shows fragmented and connected pathways at a point of connection. Blue represents the NHS reference. Green represents coordinated care. Fuchsia represents the experience of carers and people receiving support. The two rising pathways use the same geometry to illustrate a hypothesis: better coordination may create the conditions for improved recovery, independence, learning and work. The pilot tests what changes, for whom, at what cost. Conceptual model, not measured results or a forecast.
pages.20: The economic mechanism. Recovery first. Then measure the return. A transparent scenario, not a forecast: value restored paid work, then separately test any fiscal effect. One willing carer regains part-time work. Eight hours per week, at thirteen pounds an hour, for forty-eight weeks. Four thousand nine hundred and ninety-two pounds in gross annual earnings restored. Illustrative annual earnings: one person, four thousand nine hundred and ninety-two pounds. One thousand people, five million pounds. Fifty-eight thousand people, two hundred and eighty-nine point five million pounds. The public finance test: additional tax, verified tax receipts. Benefits, changes in expenditure. Service use, avoided repeat or crisis work. Cost to deliver, staff, systems and evaluation. Earnings are not cashable public savings. Gains must be demonstrated against additional costs. The one-percent scenario is arithmetic, not a forecast.
pages.21: The Casey ask. Help us test, measure and build the evidence. This demonstrator is a practical way to test whether connecting care services around people improves the experience and use of public resources. Connect services. Save time. Release capacity. Improve recovery. Support independence. Learn what works. The demonstrator will test whether it can reduce avoidable repetition, failed hand-offs and professional workload; improve recovery, independence and participation for carers and carees; release carers' capacity to care and to work where possible; use public money more effectively, with outcomes measured before claims are made; and produce a practical model that can inform national implementation. Evidence to collect: experience, capacity and outcomes. We are not asking the Commission to accept the hypothesis. Pilot first. Platform second. Evidence before scale.
pages.22: The Casey ask. Enable the test. Convene the partners. Review the evidence. A proposed oversight group: Casey Commission, convene and independently review. NHS England, digital, data and NHS App. South West London Integrated Care Board, local NHS governance. Adult social care, Richmond and Wandsworth. Housing, council and provider partners. DWP and voluntary, community and social enterprise organisations, benefits, work and community. Carers and carees, co-design and consent. Independent review, measure and publish results. What we are asking Casey to do: help convene the partnership and enable the six-month test. Protect consent, confidentiality, separate rights and clear ownership. Support an independent review and publication of the result. We are not asking Casey to accept the hypothesis. We are asking it to help us test it. Pilot first. Platform second. Evidence before scale. Connect the decisions. Improve the outcomes.
